Every family has that one board game that changes everyone's personality.
For mine, it's Monopoly.
We only play it once or twice a year, usually around the holidays.
And every single time, I mean every time, someone ends up storming off to another room.
Last month it was my brother's turn to lose it.
He'd built up a whole hotel empire on the orange properties.
He was pretty proud of it too, and he kept showing off his little plastic buildings like he'd built them with his own hands.
Then my mom landed on his space.
She looked at the rent and just laughed.
She said there was no way she was paying that much for a square with a fake hotel on it.
And she wasn't going to.
End of discussion.
My brother tried explaining the rules.
He waved the little rulebook around, but my mom had already decided the rules didn't apply to her tonight.
I guess forty years of making the rules in that house made her feel like Monopoly rules were optional too.
"You can't just decide the rent doesn't count," he said.
He sounded genuinely offended on behalf of his plastic hotels.
My mom just shrugged and slid a much smaller pile of fake money across the table, like that settled it.
He looked over at me for backup, but I just held up my hands.
I said I wasn't getting involved in whatever this was turning into.
My sister tried the same thing a minute later and got the exact same response, a shrug and a smaller pile of money.
The argument went on for a solid ten minutes.
My dad just sat there eating chips.
He was clearly enjoying the chaos a little too much.
My sister tried to mediate and read the actual rulebook out loud, but nobody was really listening by that point.
Eventually my brother picked up his hotels, one by one, and put them back in the box.
He announced that he was done playing with people who don't respect property law.
He said it with a completely straight face, and that somehow made it funnier.
We finished the game without him.
My mom won about twenty minutes later, and she still insisted she never actually broke any rules.
My brother came back for dessert like nothing happened, and nobody brought up the hotels again, not until dessert was over.
Once the pie came out, my dad couldn't resist.
He asked my mom, straight-faced, exactly how much rent she thought a slice of pie should cost.
She just laughed and said dessert, unlike Monopoly, actually had rules she was willing to follow.
